headline: The whole of Georgia lost power for nine hours

sources.title: Georgia plunges into darkness as rare nationwide blackout hits
Georgia hit by nationwide power outage

chunks.text: The lights {{went out}} across the whole of Georgia at about 00:10 on July 24. Tbilisi, Kutaisi and the breakaway region of Abkhazia all lost power [[at once]]. Georgian State Electrosystem, the national grid operator, said an emergency shutdown had caused it and that supply would return [[in stages]]. Power was fully restored at about 09:30, more than nine hours later, but the official cause is still unknown.

verbs.correct: To stop shining or working, as a light does
verbs.wrong: To be officially approved or passed

chunks.text: A national grid works as one machine, with [[supply and demand]] held in balance second by second. If a large plant or line fails, automatic protection {{kicks in}} and disconnects equipment to [[prevent]] damage, and the loss can {{knock out}} the rest of the system in seconds. In April 2025 a shutdown of the Kavkasioni transmission line left about 90 percent of consumers without power.

verbs.correct: To start to work or take effect
verbs.wrong: To create a lot of noise or fuss
To reduce a price by a small amount

chunks.text: The energy ministry in Abkhazia blamed a system failure at the Enguri hydropower plant, which supplies both Abkhazia and territory held by Georgia's central government. Tbilisi did not comment on that [[account]]. The grid operator said the exact causes were still being established. It also {{called on}} news organizations to [[rely on]] official information, saying false claims were [[circulating]]. No explanation has yet been [[confirmed]].

verbs.correct: To formally ask someone to do something
verbs.wrong: To cancel something that was planned

chunks.text: Several Tbilisi metro trains stopped inside tunnels on the night's last services, and the Tbilisi Transport Company said every passenger {{got out}} safely. Georgian Water and Power said its pumping stations {{shut down}} automatically, putting water supply [[at risk]] in Tbilisi and Rustavi, though the company said the night passed with [[minimal]] problems. Power {{came back on}} area by area, reaching parts of the capital and Kutaisi by 02:09. The rest of the country spent the night in the dark.
